title: Tenant bandwidth fences and autoscale policy orchestrator
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Goal: Deliver a pragmatic, operator-friendly orchestrator that enforces per-tenant bandwidth fences (GPU and network), applies quota backpressure, and drives autoscaling decisions that respect throughput contracts.

Problem statement: Dedicated customers require predictable throughput guarantees while sharing finite GPU clusters. Without a tightly integrated set of controls, noisy tenants can cause tail latency spikes and SLO breaches for other customers. Existing approaches (hard slicing or full isolation) are either too wasteful or operationally heavy. We need a middle-ground: soft bandwidth fences combined with a policy orchestrator that converts tenant-level contracts into runtime controls (rate limits, token buckets, burst credits, autoscale triggers, and graceful degradation strategies).

Scope:
- Implement tenant-level bandwidth fences that cover: GPU throughput (tokens/sec per tenant), KV cache eviction priority hints, and egress network egress caps for model artifact pulls.
- Add a policy orchestrator service that: translates customer throughput contracts into runtime rate-limiter configs, assigns burst credit pools, and emits autoscale signals when steady-state and burst windows are violated.
- Integrate with scheduler to prefer colocated lane groups for low-latency tenants and to relocate or rebalance tenants when starvation persists.
- Provide immediate observability: per-tenant token counters, eviction rates, tail-latency SLO deltas, and a breakdown of throttle events.

Non-goals: Full hard-slicing (1:1 GPU reservation), rewriting the runtime kernel stack, or changing model packing heuristics in this ticket.

Acceptance criteria:
- End-to-end flow from contract -> policy -> runtime config established in staging.
- Rate-limiter unit tests that simulate noisy neighbor behavior and verify isolation effectiveness (target: reduce cross-tenant P95 latency tail by >=30% under mixed load).
- Autoscale triggers demonstrated: when tenant sustained utilization >80% for 2m AND burst credit drain >70% over 30s, orchestrator generates scale-up recommendation to allocator.
- Dashboard widgets showing per-tenant fence usage and the last 72h throttle events.

Implementation approach:
1) Policy model: define a compact policy schema (throughput_limit_tokens_per_sec, burst_credits, eviction_priority_hint, autoscale_thresholds) and a controller that validates and materializes configs. Keep schema versioned and extensible.
2) Enforcement: reuse the existing rate-limiter library in runtime, extend it with per-tenant namespaces and a lightweight admission controller that can apply soft or hard limits.
3) Autoscaling: emit normalized utilization and burst-drain metrics to the existing autoscale pipeline (ENG-48294) along with a recommended instance delta. Orchestrator will not autonomously scale in this phase — it will provide recommendations and lifecycle metadata for safety reviews.
4) Telemetry: wire new Prometheus metrics and a tracing tag for fence-hit events. Expose a Console route for the new dashboard and a logging hook for audit.
5) Migration: safe rollout via canary tenants. Start with internal test tenants, then invited customers on Dedicated. Provide a kill-switch label for rapid rollback.

Risks and mitigation:
- Risk: Overly aggressive auto recommendations could trigger churn. Mitigation: recommendations are advisory for the first release and require ops approval.
- Risk: Misconfigured fences could starve legitimate traffic. Mitigation: default to conservative soft limits with visible counters and explanatory alerts.
- Risk: Complexity in policy schema. Mitigation: keep initial schema minimal and iterate based on customer feedback.

Operational playbook:
- If tenant throttle rate > 10% sustained for 10m, alert SRE and notify customer.
- For repeated eviction storms, automatically increase eviction_priority_hint and consider temporary relocation.

Deliverables:
- Controller service + schema, runtime adapter, dashboard components, unit/integration tests, rollout runbook, and docs (Confluence link in comments).
